title: Receive live birds and place on the poultry processing line

lessons.title: Receiving the truck and the birds
lessons.html:
The birds arrive

Live chickens come to the plant on trucks, packed in crates or modules. The receiving area is where your work starts. You must look after the birds well, keep records and keep yourself safe.

Before the truck arrives

  • Check that the holding area (lairage) is clean.
  • Check that fans, misters and shade are working. Birds suffer quickly in heat.
  • Have your gloves, overall, apron, boots and dust mask ready.
  • Know which farm and which flock is coming next.

When the truck arrives

  1. Guide the driver to the correct bay.
  2. Take the papers from the driver. These show the farm, the house or flock number, the number of birds, the time of loading and other flock information required by your plant.
  3. Give the papers to your supervisor or the person who checks them. Birds must not be processed until the papers are accepted.
  4. Write down the time the truck arrived.

Look at the birds

Look at the birds in the crates. Healthy birds are alert and breathe normally. Report to your supervisor straight away if you see:

  • many birds panting with open beaks (too hot);
  • birds that are wet, cold or huddled together;
  • many dead birds in the crates;
  • broken crates or birds trapped by the wings, legs or head;
  • birds that look sick, for example with swollen heads or discharge.

Dead on arrival

Birds that died on the way are called dead on arrival (DOA). Take them out of the crates, count them and put them in the correct bin for condemned birds. Write the number on the record. The farm and the plant use this number to see if catching or transport was bad.

Holding the birds

Unload the crates or modules carefully. Do not drop or throw them. Put them in the lairage in rows so that air can move between them. Keep them out of the sun and rain. Birds should not wait longer than your plant's procedure allows. Process the oldest arrivals first.

lessons.title: Handling birds kindly
lessons.html:
Animal welfare comes first

Chickens can feel pain, fear and stress. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes it a crime to treat animals cruelly. Good handling is also good for business: birds that are hurt have bruises and broken wings, and that meat must be cut off and thrown away.

Rules for handling

  • Move slowly and calmly. Do not shout.
  • Never throw, kick or hit a bird.
  • Never pull a bird out of a crate by its head, neck or one wing.
  • Hold a bird gently around the body with both hands, with the wings folded against the body.
  • Do not let birds fall onto the floor. If one escapes, catch it calmly and gently.
  • Do not overfill a crate or put things on top of the birds.

Keeping birds calm

Birds are calmer in low light. Many plants use dim or blue light in the hanging area, because chickens see blue light poorly and stay quiet. Keep noise low and avoid sudden movements. A calm bird flaps less, so there are fewer broken wings and bruises.

Hot and cold days

On hot days birds can die quickly from heat stress. Switch on fans and misters as your supervisor says. Process the birds that look most stressed first if your supervisor allows it. On cold or wet days, keep the birds out of wind and rain.

Sick or injured birds

If you see a bird with a broken leg or a bad injury, tell your supervisor immediately. It must be killed quickly and humanely by a trained person, following the plant's procedure. Do not leave it to suffer, and do not hang it on the line by a broken leg.

Why it matters

Poor handlingResult
Throwing cratesBruises, broken bones, dead birds
Pulling by one wingBroken or dislocated wings
Shouting and bright lightPanic, flapping, injuries

Every bird you handle well is less pain for the animal and less waste for the plant.

lessons.title: Hanging birds on the line safely and hygienically
lessons.html:
Shackling

Hanging birds on the moving shackle line is called shackling or hanging. The line moves at a set speed, so you must work in a steady rhythm.

How to hang a bird

  1. Take the bird out of the crate gently, holding it around the body.
  2. Hold both legs together just above the feet.
  3. Put both legs into the shackle at the same time, one leg in each side.
  4. Make sure both legs are in properly. A bird hanging by one leg is in pain and will not be stunned properly.
  5. Let go gently. The breast rub bar along the line helps keep birds calm.
  6. Fill every shackle. Empty shackles waste line time.

Do not hang

  • dead birds (they go in the DOA bin);
  • birds with broken legs;
  • birds that are very small or very sick.

Tell your supervisor about these birds and follow the plant procedure.

Hygiene

Live birds carry dust, feathers, droppings and germs such as Salmonella and Campylobacter. These germs can make people sick.

  • Wear your overall, apron, gloves and dust mask.
  • Do not eat, drink or smoke in the live bird area.
  • Wash your hands well with soap before breaks and at the end of the shift.
  • Do not walk from the live bird area into the clean area without changing and washing as the plant rules say.
  • Empty crates must go to the crate washer. Never send dirty crates back to the farm.

Your own safety

  • Keep fingers and clothes away from moving shackles, chains and conveyors.
  • Know where the emergency stop is. Use it if someone is caught or a bird is trapped.
  • Stand on the platform and do not lean over the line.
  • Hanging is repetitive work. Use the rest breaks and job rotation, and report pain in your arms, shoulders or back early.
  • Report scratches and cuts so they can be cleaned and treated.

Key points

  • Check papers and birds when the truck arrives, and count DOAs.
  • Keep birds cool, calm and out of sun and rain in the lairage.
  • Never throw birds or pull them by the head, neck or one wing.
  • Hang birds gently by both legs; do not hang dead or injured birds.
  • Wear PPE, wash your hands and know where the emergency stop is.
